overview.title: 📖 Overview: Set-Aside Lamps and Designated Objects
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 44a–44b
overview.hebrewSource: מְטַלְטְלִין נֵר חָדָשׁ אֲבָל לֹא יָשָׁן. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: כׇּל הַנֵּרוֹת מִטַּלְטְלִין, חוּץ מִן הַנֵּר הַדּוֹלֵק בְּשַׁבָּת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by confirming the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish, who permits rescuing a corpse from a fire, and by noting that Rabbi Shimon permits using oil left over in a lamp. The mishna then presents a core muktzeh dispute: may a used oil lamp be moved on Shabbat? Rabbi Yehuda forbids an old lamp as repulsive; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon forbid only a lamp that was lit that Shabbat, out of concern the flame might be disturbed; Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon is even more lenient. The Gemara maps each amora's position precisely, asks why a cup or bowl is stricter than a lamp, and closes with Rav's ruling — refined through objection — about a bed set aside for holding money.

slides.title: 🔥 Two Quick Rulings Before the Mishna
slides.label: Setting the halakha:
slides.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Sheila said in the name of Rav Asi, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish, who permits rescuing a corpse from a fire on Shabbat through an atypical, indirect method. Separately, a baraita teaches that the oil remaining in a lamp or bowl after use is forbidden — but Rabbi Shimon permits it, since in his view there is barely any prohibition of set-aside (muktzeh) at all.
slides.hebrewSource: מוֹתַר הַשֶּׁמֶן שֶׁבַּנֵּר וְשֶׁבַּקְּעָרָה אָסוּר. וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן מַתִּיר

slides.title: 💡 Which Lamps May Be Moved on Shabbat?
slides.subtitle: The Tosefta expands the mishna's brief dispute into four distinct positions
rows: An old lamp — it is repulsive from use
Any lamp not lit that Shabbat
A lamp kindled on Shabbat itself, for the whole day
A lamp still burning on Shabbat
Oil even from a still-burning lamp

callout.label: Also stated:
callout.text: Even Rabbi Shimon agrees that a cup, bowl, or lantern full of oil may not be moved from its place, even after the flame goes out.

slides.title: 👨‍👦 Abaye Maps Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon's View
slides.subtitle: He follows his father in one point, and disagrees in another

steps.content: 1️⃣ Agrees with his father, Rabbi Shimon: there is no general prohibition of set-aside (muktzeh) for lamps
2️⃣ Rabbi Shimon's own limit: only once the flame is extinguished may the lamp be moved — while lit, no
3️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon disagrees here: even while the lamp is still burning, one may draw oil from it or move it
4️⃣ His reasoning: doing so is in no way considered an act of extinguishing the flame

callout.label: Why 'however' (aval)?
callout.text: Ulla explains the Tosefta's stricter clause about cup/bowl/lantern returns to Rabbi Yehuda's position; Mar Zutra rejects this and says it is Rabbi Shimon's own distinction between a small lamp he expects to go out and a large vessel he doesn't.

slides.title: 🍷 Why Are a Cup and Bowl Stricter Than a Lamp?
slides.subtitle: Ulla and Mar Zutra propose different explanations

lines.speaker: Ulla
lines.text: The Tosefta's phrase 'however, a cup, bowl, and lantern' switches back to explaining Rabbi Yehuda's stricter opinion, not Rabbi Shimon's.

lines.speaker: Mar Zutra
lines.text: That can't be right — Rabbi Yehuda already forbids moving any used lamp! Why would the word 'however' be needed to add a bowl?

lines.speaker: Mar Zutra
lines.text: Rather, it is Rabbi Shimon speaking: he permitted only a small lamp, since he already expects it to go out that day. A large cup, bowl, or lantern holds too much oil to expect it extinguished — he sets it aside for all of Shabbat.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Zeira
lines.text: A metal candlestick (pamot) lit on Shabbat: everyone agrees it is forbidden — since it was actually kindled, both those set-aside due to disgust and those set-aside due to prohibition apply.

slides.title: 💰 A Bed Designated for Money
slides.subtitle: Rav's ruling, challenged and refined through the mishna's own logic

nodes.content: 📜 Rav (via Rav Yehuda): a bed designated to hold money may not be moved on Shabbat
❓ Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: our mishna permits moving a new lamp — even though it's designated for lighting! Shouldn't a bed, not even designated that way, be more lenient?

columns.label: Designated + money on it
columns.content: Forbidden to move — even if the money is later removed, if it was there during twilight

columns.label: Designated, no money now
columns.content: Permitted to move, so long as no money was there at twilight (bein hashemashot)

nodes.content: ✅ Refined rule: the bed's status is fixed by whether money sat on it during twilight, not merely by its designation alone

summary.principle: Whether a lamp, bed, or wagon may be moved on Shabbat depends on precisely why it was set aside — disgust, an ongoing prohibition (a burning flame), or an object resting on it at twilight — and each amora draws that line in a slightly different place.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 Halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish on rescuing a corpse; Rabbi Shimon permits leftover oil
💡 Mishna/Tosefta: four graded positions on moving lamps, from Rabbi Yehuda's strictness to Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Shimon's leniency

columns.content: 🍷 Cup/bowl/lantern stay forbidden even once extinguished — too large to expect
💰 A money-bed's status is fixed by twilight, not designation alone

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an object becomes muktzeh through disgust, active prohibition, or what rested on it at twilight — and each cause has its own scope

quiz.q: According to the halakha as stated on this daf, whose opinion is followed regarding rescuing a corpse from a fire on Shabbat?
o: Rabbi Yehuda
Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish, who permits it
Rabbi Meir
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda ben Sheila said in the name of Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish, who permits rescuing a corpse from fire.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, why does Rabbi Yehuda forbid moving an old oil lamp on Shabbat?
o: It might still be hot
It is covered in soot and considered repulsive, hence set aside from use
It belongs to someone else
It was lit that day
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda holds that an old, sooty lamp is set aside due to its disgusting nature (muktzeh machamat mi'us), unlike a new lamp.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon's opinion differ from that of his father, Rabbi Shimon, regarding a still-burning lamp?
o: He forbids moving any lamp at all
He permits drawing oil or moving the lamp even while it is still burning, since he holds this is not comparable to extinguishing it
He agrees completely with his father
He follows Rabbi Yehuda instead
quiz.e: Abaye explains that while both agree there is no general muktzeh for lamps, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon goes further than his father and permits use even before the flame is extinguished.

quiz.q: According to Mar Zutra, why does even Rabbi Shimon forbid moving a cup, bowl, or lantern full of oil, even after the flame is extinguished?
o: They are always considered disgusting
A small lamp is expected to burn out that day, but a large vessel with much oil is not expected to be extinguished and is set aside for all of Shabbat
Only priests may move them
Rabbi Shimon never permits moving any vessel
quiz.e: Mar Zutra explains Rabbi Shimon's leniency was limited to a small lamp he has in mind to go out; large vessels like a cup or bowl are set aside for the whole of Shabbat.

quiz.q: Regarding a bed designated to hold money, when is it prohibited to move it on Shabbat, according to the refined version of Rav's ruling?
o: Only if it was designated for money and money is currently on it, or money was on it during twilight (bein hashemashot)
It is always forbidden to move any bed
Only if the bed is new
Beds may never hold money at all
quiz.e: The refined ruling distinguishes: a designated bed with money currently on it is forbidden; without money now, it's permitted unless money was present at twilight, which fixes its set-aside status for the whole day.
